questions.prompt: Which statement correctly defines what a Linux distribution ("distro") actually is?
options: A complete, installable operating system that bundles the Linux kernel with userland tools, a package manager, and default configuration
The Linux kernel itself, with no additional software bundled in
A virtual machine image that only runs inside WSL2
A specific version of the GNU Project's compiler toolchain
A proprietary fork of Windows Server that mimics Linux commands
It's the default group assigned to every new file, separate from chown
questions.explain: A distribution is a company or community's bundle of the Linux kernel plus userland tools, a package manager, default configuration, and often a support model. Ubuntu, RHEL, and Debian are all different distributions wrapped around the same underlying kernel family.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B collapses the distinction the lesson is built on: the kernel by itself has no shell, no package manager, and no utilities you'd sit down and use. A distribution is specifically what gets built on top of the kernel to make it a usable operating system — the kernel alone isn't one.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: both the Linux kernel and most GNU tools are released under the ________, an open-source license guaranteeing the source code stays free to read, modify, and redistribute.
questions.explain: The GPL (GNU General Public License) is the open-source license under which the kernel and most GNU tools are released. It's exactly why a company can run Linux on hundreds of servers without paying a licensing fee — a decisive factor compared to per-core commercial OS licensing at scale.

questions.code:
$ ls -la /
lrwxrwxrwx   1 root root     7 Jun 22  2023 bin -> usr/bin
questions.prompt: Running `ls -la /` on a modern Ubuntu server shows `bin -> usr/bin` as a symlink rather than a real directory. What does this indicate?
options: Modern Ubuntu merged /bin into /usr/bin and kept /bin as a symlink so old hardcoded paths still work
The system is missing its real /bin directory because of a failed install
Every directory listed directly under / is required to be a symlink
/usr/bin is a temporary mount that disappears on the next reboot
questions.explain: Modern distributions merged /bin into /usr/bin, keeping /bin (and /sbin) as symlinks purely so that scripts and tools hardcoded to the old paths keep working. The FHS layout holding true across every machine is exactly what lets automation tooling rely on it.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of setting up a local VirtualBox lab VM, per Lesson 3, in the correct order.
items: Download the Ubuntu Server ISO from ubuntu.com
Install Oracle VirtualBox (or VMware Workstation Player)
Create a new VM with at least 2 GB RAM and 20 GB disk
Attach the ISO to the new VM
Boot the VM and complete the Ubuntu Server installer
questions.explain: Lesson 3 walks through exactly this order for a local VM: get the installer image, get the hypervisor installed, provision a VM with adequate resources, attach the ISO as its boot media, and then actually run the installer — the end result behaves exactly like a standalone physical server.

questions.code:
$ cp app app_backup
cp: -r not specified; omitting directory 'app'
questions.prompt: Why does this cp command fail?
options: cp refuses to copy a directory unless -r (recursive) is explicitly given
app_backup already exists, and cp won't overwrite a directory
cp requires the destination to already exist as a directory first
cp can only copy files that end in a recognized file extension
questions.explain: Copying a directory tree requires the -r flag — without it, cp refuses and tells you so directly, rather than silently doing something unexpected. `cp -r app app_backup` is the fix.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about cat, less, head, and tail, per Lesson 7.
options: less loads a file for paged, searchable viewing without needing to read the whole file into scrollback first
cat is the better tool than less for interactively viewing a multi-thousand-line log file
tail -f keeps running and prints new lines as they're appended, until stopped with Ctrl+C
head shows the last 10 lines of a file by default
wc -l counts the number of lines in a file
questions.explain: less pages through a file without needing it fully loaded, which is exactly why it's the standard tool for large files — cat just floods the terminal and scrolls past before you can read it. tail -f follows a growing file live until you stop it. head shows the first 10 lines by default, not the last — tail is the one that shows the last 10. wc -l reports a line count.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ls -li on two hard-linked files shows the same ________ number for both, confirming they point at the exact same underlying data on disk.
questions.explain: A hard link is a second name pointing at the same data on disk. Both names share the same inode number, and the link count shown by ls -l increases — the file only disappears once every name pointing to that inode is removed.

questions.prompt: An admin means to run `rm -rf ./app_backup/` but a stray space turns it into `rm -rf / app_backup/`. What actually happens?
options: rm -rf treats / and app_backup/ as two separate targets and attempts to recursively delete the entire root filesystem, plus app_backup/
Linux detects the dangerous pattern automatically and refuses to run the command
Only app_backup/ is deleted; the stray space before it is silently ignored
The command fails with a syntax error and nothing is deleted
questions.explain: The shell splits arguments on whitespace, so a stray space turns one path into two separate arguments — / and app_backup/ — and rm -rf (recursive, force, no confirmation) will attempt to delete both with no warning and no undo. This is exactly why the lesson calls rm -rf one of the most dangerous things you can type as root.

questions.prompt: What does a Linux umask value actually do?
options: It's a bitmask subtracted from the starting permissions (666 for files, 777 for directories) to determine the default permissions a newly created file or directory gets
It sets the maximum file size a user is allowed to create
It encrypts new files automatically until chmod is run on them
It determines which users are allowed to run chmod at all
It sets the default group ownership assigned to every new file
It controls how many hard links a file can have before Linux blocks a new one
questions.explain: umask is subtracted from the starting point of 666 for files and 777 for directories. With the common default of 022, that's 666-022=644 for a new file and 777-022=755 for a new directory — files never get the execute bit by default, even with a permissive umask.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E sounds plausible because a directory's setgid bit genuinely does make new files inherit a group — but that's setgid's job specifically, not umask's. umask only ever adjusts the rwx permission bits on a new file or directory; it has no effect on which user or group ends up owning it.

questions.prompt: Based on this permission string, what can a member of the ops group (who isn't mchen) actually do with deploy.sh?
options: Read and execute it, but not write to it
Read, write, and execute it, exactly like the owner
Nothing at all — only the owner has any access
Write to it but not execute it
questions.explain: The permission string rwxr-x--- breaks into three triplets: owner has rwx (read/write/execute), group has r-x (read/execute, no write), and other has nothing. A non-owner member of the ops group falls into the group triplet, so they can read and execute deploy.sh but not modify it.

questions.prompt: Match each account-related file or concept to what it actually is, per Lesson 11.
right: Root-only file holding salted password hashes and password-aging rules
The numeric identifiers Linux actually checks internally, with usernames as a human-readable layer on top
World-readable file listing each account's username, UID, GID, home directory, and shell
File listing each group's GID and its supplementary members
questions.explain: /etc/passwd is world-readable and lists the account roster — username, UID, GID, home directory, shell — with an 'x' placeholder where a password hash would be. /etc/shadow actually holds the hashed password and is root-only. /etc/group lists each group's GID and supplementary members. UID/GID are the numeric values Linux checks internally, with names in passwd/group as the human-readable layer on top.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about setuid, setgid, and the sticky bit, per Lesson 13.
options: setuid on an executable makes it run with the privileges of the file's owner, not the user who launched it
setgid on a directory makes new files created inside automatically inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group
The sticky bit on a directory lets any user with write access delete any other user's files inside it
setuid has a meaningful effect when applied to a directory, the same way setgid does
chmod 4755 sets the setuid bit in addition to rwxr-xr-x permissions
questions.explain: setuid makes an executable run as its owner — exactly how passwd lets an ordinary user update their own password despite /etc/shadow being root-only. setgid on a directory makes new contents inherit that directory's group. The sticky bit does the opposite of option C: it restricts deletion to the file's owner (or root), which is exactly what protects a shared directory like /tmp. setuid on a directory has no effect at all, unlike setgid. 4755 correctly combines the leading setuid digit (4) with 755.

questions.prompt: A developer wrote this redirection intending to capture both stdout and stderr in deploy.log. What actually happens?
options: stderr still prints to the terminal, because 2>&1 merges stderr into wherever stdout was pointing at that moment — which was still the terminal when 2>&1 ran
Both stdout and stderr land correctly in deploy.log, exactly as intended
Only stderr is written to deploy.log; stdout is discarded entirely
The shell raises a syntax error because 2>&1 must be the very first redirection on the line
questions.explain: 2>&1 only works correctly when it comes after the stdout redirection, because it copies wherever stdout is pointed at the moment it runs — not wherever stdout ends up later in the line. Here 2>&1 runs before > redirects stdout to the file, so stderr gets merged into the terminal, and only stdout ends up in deploy.log. The fix is `> deploy.log 2>&1`.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: running sed 's/old/new/' file.conf alone only prints the changed result to the terminal; adding the ________ flag edits the file in place.
questions.explain: Without -i, sed previews the change by printing the result without touching the file. Adding -i edits the file directly — exactly how an ops team flips a setting across a config file without opening an editor.

questions.prompt: What does this command actually match?
options: Regular files under /tmp whose content hasn't been modified in more than 30 days
Regular files under /tmp that are smaller than 30 MB
Every file and directory under /tmp, sorted by age
Files that will expire automatically in 30 days from now
questions.explain: -type f restricts matches to regular files (excluding directories), and -mtime +30 filters to files whose content hasn't changed in more than 30 days — exactly the kind of stale temp file worth cleaning up, per Lesson 16.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a plain assignment like APP_ENV=production is only visible in the current shell; adding ________ in front of the assignment makes every child process spawned afterward inherit it too.
questions.explain: A plain shell variable stays local to the current shell. export marks it so every process launched from that shell afterward inherits it — which is exactly why a deploy script reading $APP_ENV sees nothing unless the variable was exported first.

questions.prompt: This sends SIGKILL to PID 2210 instead of the default SIGTERM. What's the practical difference?
options: SIGKILL terminates the process immediately and it cannot catch it, close open files, or clean up first — unlike SIGTERM, which it can catch and handle gracefully
SIGKILL and SIGTERM behave identically; -9 is just a shorthand spelling
SIGKILL only works on background jobs, never on a process running in the foreground
SIGKILL asks the process to shut down nicely, while SIGTERM forces it immediately
questions.explain: SIGTERM (signal 15, the default) is a request a process can catch and respond to — closing files and exiting gracefully. SIGKILL (signal 9) is not a request; the kernel terminates the process immediately and it cannot catch, ignore, or clean up after it. The lesson's advice is to always try SIGTERM first and reserve SIGKILL for a process that's already ignoring it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about systemctl enable vs. start, per Lesson 19.
options: systemctl start runs a service immediately but has no effect on whether it starts automatically at the next reboot
systemctl enable creates a symlink so the service starts at boot, without changing whether it's currently running
systemctl enable --now both enables a service for boot and starts it immediately
systemctl disable immediately stops a currently running service
Restart=on-failure in a unit file is what makes systemd restart a crashed service automatically
questions.explain: start and enable control two separate things: start affects only the current running state, and enable only affects the boot-time symlink. enable --now does both at once. disable removes the boot-time symlink but, per the lesson, does not stop a service that's currently running. Restart=on-failure is the directive that actually makes systemd restart a crashed process automatically.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of setting up a systemd timer, per Lesson 20, in the correct order.
items: Write the paired .service unit with Type=oneshot and an ExecStart command
Write the .timer unit with an OnCalendar= schedule and Persistent=true
Run systemctl enable --now on the .timer unit
Confirm the schedule with systemctl list-timers
questions.explain: A systemd timer needs two files sharing the same base name: the .service unit defining what to run (as a one-time oneshot job), and the .timer unit defining when. Only after both exist does enabling the timer make sense, and list-timers is how you confirm it actually took effect.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on free -h output, a server can show low 'free' memory but still have plenty of headroom, because the ________ column already accounts for reclaimable buff/cache — that's the number that actually indicates memory pressure.
questions.explain: buff/cache is memory the kernel is using to cache disk data, reclaimed instantly if an application needs it. 'available' is the column that already factors that in, which is why a server showing low 'free' but high 'available' is not actually short on memory.

questions.prompt: Match each apt command to its dnf equivalent, per Lesson 23's mapping table.
questions.explain: apt install maps to dnf install, apt remove maps to dnf remove, apt search maps to dnf search, and apt list --installed maps to dnf list installed — the same underlying job, different family-specific syntax.

questions.prompt: /etc/fstab references the new /data filesystem by UUID rather than by its device name, /dev/sdb1. Why?
options: A UUID uniquely identifies the filesystem itself and stays stable even if the device name shifts after a disk is added or removed; a device name like /dev/sdb1 can change
Device names like /dev/sdb1 aren't valid syntax inside /etc/fstab at all
Referencing a UUID makes the filesystem mount faster at boot than a device name would
/etc/fstab requires a UUID specifically for ext4 filesystems, but not for other filesystem types
questions.explain: Device names can shift if a disk is added or removed, but a UUID never changes — which is exactly why /etc/fstab references filesystems by UUID rather than a device path, per Lesson 24.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about SSH hardening and firewall setup, per Lesson 26.
options: PasswordAuthentication no forces every login to use a trusted private key instead of a password
ufw allow OpenSSH should run before ufw enable, or you risk locking yourself out the moment the firewall activates
PermitRootLogin no has no real security benefit once PasswordAuthentication no is already set
--permanent on a firewalld rule makes it persist across reboots; firewall-cmd --reload is still needed to apply it without dropping active connections
Regularly running apt upgrade or dnf update is a cosmetic habit with little real security benefit
questions.explain: Disabling password auth forces key-only login. Allowing SSH before enabling a default-deny firewall is essential, since enabling it first drops your own connection. --permanent plus --reload is exactly how firewalld rules are made to persist without dropping active sessions. PermitRootLogin no still matters on its own: it forces every login through a named account and sudo, making privileged actions attributable to a real person — that's independent of password auth. Patching regularly closes known vulnerabilities before they're exploited, which the lesson calls just as important as any single setting.

questions.code:
#!/bin/bash
set -e

echo "Starting backup..."
cp /nonexistent/file /var/backups/
echo "This line never runs"
questions.prompt: With set -e active, what happens when the cp command fails partway through this script?
options: The script exits immediately at the failed cp command, so the final echo never runs
Bash prints a warning about the failed cp but continues on to run the final echo
set -e only affects commands inside a pipeline, so this script behaves the same with or without it
The script automatically retries cp up to three times before giving up
questions.explain: set -e changes Bash's default behavior of continuing after a failed command — the script now exits the instant any command returns a nonzero status, which is why the comment line 'This line never runs' is accurate here.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the first line of a Bash script, #!/bin/bash, is called a ________ — it tells the kernel which interpreter should run the rest of the file.
questions.explain: The shebang (#!) is read by the kernel before anything else in the file, and it hands the script to the named interpreter (/bin/bash) to execute line by line. Without it, a script might fall back to a shell that doesn't support Bash-specific syntax.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Bash tests and argument handling, per Lessons 28 and 30.
options: [[ ]] doesn't word-split or glob-expand unquoted variables inside it, unlike [ ]
-eq compares numeric values, while == compares strings literally
shift drops $1 and renumbers the remaining positional parameters down by one
getopts requires every flag to accept a value; a flag with no value, like -v, isn't supported
[ ] is really a call to the test command under the hood
questions.explain: [[ ]] is Bash's more forgiving extended test syntax, specifically safer with unquoted variables than [ ]. -eq is for numeric comparisons; == compares strings. shift renumbers remaining arguments down by one, letting a script loop through an unknown count of them. [ ] is literally the test command. getopts does support value-less flags: in the getopts string, a colon after a letter means that flag takes a value, and no colon means it's a plain on/off flag — v (no colon) works exactly as a toggle, which is the opposite of what option D claims.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the trap-based cleanup pattern, per Lesson 31, in the correct order.
items: A temporary file is created with mktemp and its path stored in a variable
trap 'rm -f "$tmpfile"' EXIT registers the cleanup command
The rest of the script runs, including logic that might fail at any point
The script exits, whether normally, via exit, or killed by Ctrl-C
The trapped cleanup command runs automatically, removing the temporary file
questions.explain: The temp file is created first, then the trap is registered right away — before any logic that could fail. Whatever happens next, the moment the script exits for any reason, EXIT fires the trapped command automatically, guaranteeing the temp file gets removed even if the script failed partway through.

questions.prompt: The capstone checklist insists ufw allow OpenSSH must run before ufw enable. What would happen if the order were reversed, on a server you're only connected to over SSH?
options: Enabling the default-deny firewall before any allow rule exists would immediately drop your own SSH connection, locking you out
Nothing different happens — ufw always allows whichever connection enabled it
ufw would refuse to enable at all until an allow rule exists
The current SSH connection stays open, but all future connections would be blocked until a reboot
questions.explain: A default-deny firewall blocks everything not explicitly allowed the moment it's enabled, including the very SSH connection you're using to administer the server. Allowing OpenSSH first, then enabling the firewall, is exactly the order the capstone's kickoff lesson calls out as mattering.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the capstone's final verification checklist, per Lesson 34.
options: systemctl is-enabled northbridge-tool confirms the service starts on boot, while systemctl is-active confirms it's running right now — they check two different things
sudo sshd -T | grep -i permitrootlogin confirms whether the running sshd config actually has root login disabled
Seeing 'Accepted publickey' entries in the SSH logs, with no accepted root logins, confirms the hardening is actually working, not just configured
A hardened server is fully verified as soon as sshd_config contains the right lines, without needing to check the logs at all
sudo crontab -u deploy -l is unrelated to verifying the capstone's cron requirement
questions.explain: is-enabled and is-active check boot-time configuration and current runtime state respectively — genuinely different things. sshd -T reads the running effective configuration, confirming the setting actually took effect. Checking the logs for accepted publickey entries and the absence of root logins is exactly the verification step the lesson emphasizes as separating 'configured' from 'actually working.' Checking sshd_config's text alone isn't enough — that's exactly why the checklist insists on log review. And crontab -u deploy -l is precisely how you verify the capstone's nightly cron job requirement, not something unrelated to it.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the full capstone build, per Lessons 32 and 33, in the correct order.
items: Create the deploy user and confirm sudo access actually works before relying on it
Generate an SSH key pair and confirm key-based login works in a new terminal
Disable PermitRootLogin and PasswordAuthentication in sshd_config, keeping the existing session open
Allow OpenSSH in ufw, then enable the firewall
Wrap the internal tool in a systemd service and enable it
Schedule the nightly cron job and review the logs to confirm everything is working
questions.explain: Each step depends on the one before it holding up: sudo access is confirmed before root login is ever disabled, key-based login is confirmed before password authentication is turned off, and SSH is allowed in the firewall before the firewall itself is enabled. Only once the server is reachable and locked down does it make sense to add the managed service, the scheduled job, and finally confirm all of it in the logs.
